title: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (India, INASL)
subject: gastroenterology
setting: Primary care, diabetes clinic, gastroenterology and hepatology outpatients
summary: MASLD is steatosis with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (Asian Indian cut-offs) and limited alcohol. Stage fibrosis with FIB-4 or APRI and refer indeterminate or high results for VCTE. Treat with 7 to 10% weight loss and at least 200 minutes a week of exercise; consider vitamin E, pioglitazone or saroglitazar for steatohepatitis with F1 to F3 fibrosis.

sections.title: Define (INASL 2025 adoption of MASLD)
items: MASLD: steatosis (5% or more of hepatocytes, usually seen on ultrasound) plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, with alcohol below 30 g/day in men and below 20 g/day in women.

Asian Indian cardiometabolic criteria: BMI 23 kg/m2 or more (25 or more is obesity) or waist above 90 cm (men) or 80 cm (women); fasting glucose 100 mg/dL or more or HbA1c 5.7% or more; BP 130/85 mmHg or more; triglycerides 150 mg/dL or more; HDL 40 mg/dL or less (men) or 50 mg/dL or less (women).

MetALD: steatosis with a cardiometabolic risk factor and moderate alcohol (men over 30 to below 60 g/day, or 210 to 420 g/week; women over 20 to below 50 g/day, or 140 to 350 g/week). INASL makes no drug recommendation for MetALD.
Lean MASLD in Indians: BMI below 23 kg/m2 with normal waist (below 90 cm men, 80 cm women).
High-risk groups to evaluate: type 2 diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome.
Exclude other causes: significant alcohol, hepatitis B and C, drugs, and other chronic liver diseases, which can coexist with MASLD.

sections.title: Stage fibrosis stepwise
items: Primary and secondary care: calculate FIB-4 and APRI. FIB-4 below 1.3 (APRI below 0.5) makes advanced fibrosis unlikely; FIB-4 1.3 to 2.67 (APRI 0.5 to 2.0) is indeterminate; FIB-4 above 2.67 (APRI above 2.0) suggests advanced fibrosis.
Refer intermediate, high or discordant results to tertiary care for vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE).

VCTE liver stiffness: below 6.0 kPa makes significant fibrosis unlikely; 8.2 kPa or more suggests significant fibrosis (F2); 9.7 kPa or more advanced fibrosis (F3); 13.6 kPa or more cirrhosis. 20 kPa or more, especially with low platelets, suggests clinically significant portal hypertension.
CAP above 275 dB/m on VCTE indicates steatosis (EASL threshold cited by INASL).
Evaluate every patient with steatohepatitis, advanced fibrosis or diabetes for cardiovascular disease, and consider kidney function testing.

sections.title: Lifestyle: the main treatment
items: Overweight or obese: lose 7 to 10% of baseline weight by diet and exercise; about 3 to 5% improves steatosis, 7% or more steatohepatitis and 10% or more fibrosis.

Restrict daily calories by 30% or by 500 to 1000 kcal. Keep total fat below 30% of energy, saturated fat below 10%, trans fat below 1% and free sugars below 10% (ideally below 5%); cut fructose and sweetened drinks.
Moderate-intensity aerobic or resistance exercise 30 to 45 minutes a day on at least 5 days (at least 200 minutes a week) for all patients, including lean MASLD.
The INASL NAFLD guidance treats alcohol above 20 g/day as significant in Indian men and women; advise minimising alcohol, and manage heavier intake as MetALD or alcohol-related disease.
Treat the metabolic drivers: diabetes, dyslipidaemia and hypertension. Statins are safe in MASLD even with raised transaminases; be cautious in decompensated cirrhosis.

sections.title: Drugs for steatohepatitis with F1 to F3 fibrosis
items: Vitamin E 800 IU/day in 2 divided doses (course of 2 years) for non-diabetic adults with steatohepatitis. Long-term risks include prostate cancer and haemorrhagic stroke.
Pioglitazone 30 mg/day (course of 2 years) for steatohepatitis in diabetic or non-diabetic adults. Watch for weight gain and bone loss in women.
Saroglitazar 4 mg/day (course of 1 year) for steatohepatitis in diabetic or non-diabetic adults (weak recommendation).

Metformin improves liver tests but not histology and is not a liver-specific treatment. INASL advises against obeticholic acid; SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs (liraglutide, semaglutide) are promising but not yet recommended as liver-specific therapy.
Bariatric surgery is not a primary treatment for MASLD, but when indicated for obesity it can be done in non-cirrhotic disease; use caution in compensated and avoid in decompensated cirrhosis.

sections.title: Follow-up and cirrhosis care
items: Repeat non-invasive fibrosis tests periodically to track progression, and review weight, glucose, lipids and BP at each visit.
MASH cirrhosis: ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein every 6 months for hepatocellular carcinoma, and manage portal hypertension per cirrhosis guidance.
Refer to a hepatologist for advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, discordant tests, or diagnostic doubt (biopsy).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using Western BMI cut-offs: Indians develop MASLD at BMI 23 kg/m2 and even below (lean MASLD).
Relying on transaminases: normal ALT does not exclude steatohepatitis or fibrosis.
Stopping statins in MASLD because of mildly raised enzymes.
Giving vitamin E to people with diabetes or using drugs in MetALD without addressing alcohol.
Forgetting to evaluate for cardiovascular disease in steatohepatitis, advanced fibrosis or diabetes, as INASL recommends.

drugs.name: Vitamin E
drugs.notes: Non-diabetic adults with steatohepatitis and F1 to F3 fibrosis; course of 2 years.

drugs.name: Pioglitazone
drugs.notes: Steatohepatitis with F1 to F3, with or without diabetes; weight gain, bone loss.

drugs.name: Saroglitazar
drugs.notes: Steatohepatitis with F1 to F3, with or without diabetes; course of 1 year (weak recommendation).
